title: Savings void
spec: U07 · the compression that fails its answer key
intro: The cheapest answer on the whole grid for this question is also wrong. Watch a 88% saving get voided by one missing fact, and learn the assertion that catches it.
foot: Do it for real: Compare drawer, Q9, budgeted vs compressed

steps.title: Two compressors, same question
narrative: Budgeted and compressed are both COMPRESS-family strategies, and they attack the same layer. They differ in how: budgeted evicts whole records until it fits a cap; compressed rewrites records into a shorter abstract.
On Q9 — summarize M-2001's authorization history — budgeted lands at 565 tokens and compressed at 208. On tokens alone, compressed wins by a mile.
steps.youDo: Open the Compare drawer, pin Q9, and set the two columns to budgeted and compressed.

steps.title: Read the two answers, not the two totals
narrative: Budgeted says: two requests, PA-1001 approved at score 100, PA-1004 in manual review at score 65. Correct.
Compressed says: two requests, PA-1001 approved, "her history shows consistent approvals." The abstract step summarised away the request that was not approved — and then editorialised in its place.
steps.claudeSays: Nothing went wrong in the model. The compressor handed it a context in which PA-1004's outcome no longer existed, and it answered faithfully from what it was given.

Member M-2001 (Rosa Delgado) has 2 authorization requests:
PA-1001 was APPROVED. Her history shows consistent approvals.
⏸  GRADING against the Q9 answer key
✕ FAILED — missing required facts: PA-1004, MANUAL_REVIEW

view.text: "Member M-2001 has 2 authorization requests: PA-1001 APPROVED (score 100); PA-1004 MANUAL_REVIEW (score 65)." — both required facts present.

views.text: "Member M-2001 (Rosa Delgado) has 2 authorization requests: PA-1001 was APPROVED. Her history shows consistent approvals."

steps.title: The stamp that voids the saving
narrative: The receipt does not congratulate compressed on 208 tokens. It stamps it ✕ FAILED — savings void and names the facts that went missing.

This is the one rule the whole course rests on: a saving that changes the answer is not a saving. It is a defect with a smaller bill. In a prior-authorization system, "consistent approvals" about a member with a pending manual review is not a rounding error — it is the wrong clinical picture.

before.title: THE CHEAPEST WRONG ANSWER ON THE GRID

steps.title: The fidelity assertion
narrative: The fix is not "compress less". It is to make compression prove it kept what mattered. Before an abstract is allowed into the context, assert that every identifier and status present in the source survives into the summary.
Turn the assertion on and compressed stops returning a cheap wrong answer — it returns a slightly more expensive right one, because the assertion forces the outcome fields to be carried verbatim.
steps.youDo: In the U07 lab, break it on purpose: disable the assertion, re-ask Q9, and watch the FAILED stamp come back.

lines: return text            # ships whatever the summariser produced
missing  = [f for f in required if f not in text]
return extract_verbatim(records, keep=missing)  # fall back a rung

steps.title: What to take to the router
narrative: Compression is not disqualified — it is conditional. On questions whose answer is a shape rather than a set of identifiers, abstracting is exactly right. On aggregation questions with named facts in the key, it is the most dangerous strategy on the toggle bar.
That distinction, made per question class from measured evidence, is what U12's router is built out of. Never route to an arm that fails the key on that class — however good its tokens look.
